messages:
alex: Quick RFC follow-up — proposing a small, targeted design for staged backpressure/penalty tiers and the admission interface. Came out of yesterday's sync when we worried that a single "hard" throttle is too disruptive.

maya: > +1 to staged. Can you sketch the signal flow? especially how we move from soft-shed -> penalty -> harder throttle without oscillation. :thinking_face:

alex: Sketch: 1) admission checks use a decoupled Admission API that returns verdicts: ALLOW / SOFT_CAP / PENDING_PENALTY / BLOCK. 2) A short-lived penalty state map per-tenant (ttl ~ 30s) with a penalty level (0..N). 3) Router enforces SOFT_CAP by reducing batch size & preferring cheaper variants; PENDING_PENALTY reduces token budget; BLOCK is last resort. 4) Signals to escalate are sustained token-rate above threshold, high error rate, or abuse heuristics.

jordy: How is this different from current quota bucketing? sounds similar but we need clear separation between "accounting quotas" and "admission verdicts".

alex: Exactly — quotas remain accounting (monthly/daily units). Admission decisions are runtime and transient. We should avoid exhausting quota store calls in the hot path. So: admission API should use local cache + probabilistic probe to quota-store. If the cache is cold, return PENDING_PENALTY and trigger async verification.

sam: That async verification bit worries me — how do we avoid races where clients get inconsistent responses? e.g., first request gets ALLOW then next gets BLOCK when probe returns.

maya: We should make the probe only affect subsequent requests, never retroactively revoke a token already issued. Consistency model: optimistic allow + eventual reconcile. If probe fails and we overissued, we mark tenant for short penalty window.

alex: Right. Tradeoff doc short: fast path = local admission decision (cheap, low latency). Slow path = probed/authoritative check. Overissue -> short penalty -> instrumentation to alert.

jordy: Can we get a small config example? e.g., penalty decay / escalation thresholds?

alex: Sure — proposal config snippet: 
```
penalty_policy: 
  levels: [soft, moderate, strict]
  duration_s: [30, 120, 600]
  escalate_after_secs: 20  # sustained violation window
  deescalate_if_below: 0.8  # usage fraction below threshold
  soft_cap_multiplier: 0.6  # allowed tokens vs requested
```

sam: Telemetry we need: admission_verdict, penalty_level, probe_latency, overissue_count, degrade_actions_taken. Also link to request id so we can trace cascades.

maya: Ops playbook idea: start with penality-only mode (no BLOCK) in a canary region for 72h, then enable BLOCK for tier-3 offenders. We'll run two weeks with synthetic heavy tenants to validate.

jordy: Implementation boundary question: who owns the stateful penalty map? candidates: router sidecar, admission service, or distributed cache (redis). My vote: keep it co-located in admission service but sharded per-region to minimize cross-region flapping.

alex: Agreed. Admission service owns penalty map. Router caches verdicts for short ttl (5s) to avoid thundering herd. On cache miss, router queries admission.

sam: Security/abuse concern: attackers could try to game escalation heuristics by spiking low-volume bursts across many tenants. Need signal aggregation across correlated actors and device fingerprints. Add abuse heuristics like "spike-pattern similarity" and gradient-based anomaly detectors.

alex: We'll add a flag to mark "suspected-abuse" which increases penalty escalation sensitivity. Detection lives in abuse-detector (ML) that emits events to admission service.

deploy-bot: rolling-deploy: admission-service v2 -> canary (region=us-west-2) started at 1718004720.

maya: Rollout plan: 1) feature-flagged admission-service in canary with policy in observe-only (emit verdicts but don't enforce) for 48h. 2) flip to soft enforcement (SOFT_CAP) another 48h. 3) enable escalation windows + penalties in staged fashion. 4) enable BLOCK only for top offenders behind manual rollback.

jordy: One more boundary callout: SDK/edge clients still expect HTTP 429 for throttling. We should map verdicts -> HTTP codes: ALLOW=200, SOFT_CAP=200+warning-header, PENDING_PENALTY=202? or 200 with header?, BLOCK=429 + body. Thoughts?

sam: I'd avoid 202 for admission — it's confusing. Prefer: soft_cap returns 200 with X-Redwood-Warning + reduced quota info; block returns 429. PENDING_PENALTY should generally be treated like soft_cap from client perspective.

alex: Agreed. Also include guidance for SDKs to expose a 'penalty_level' field and backoff hints. That will make client-side smoothing possible.

maya: OK this is actionable. Next steps: alex to open a short RFC PR with config schema + telemetry table + rollout checklist. jordy to prototype admission cache behavior. sam to list telemetry dashboards and alerts. I'll coordinate canary windows with infra. :rocket:

alex: Thanks. I'll draft the PR today and link here.

srebot: alert: canary admission-service v2 saw 0.3% overissue rate at 1718005200, spike pattern matches synthetic-test-suite 7.

alex: Noted — adding synthetic suite into canary tests.

maya: :thumbsup:
